title: StableCore reserved GPU ramp & isolation check
summary: Initial scoping call to understand StableCore's inference load profile, isolation requirements, and burst patterns. Focus on reserved pool sizing, hot-pool pre-warm, and options for private deployment vs Redwood Dedicated. Action items include modeling surge scenarios and sharing security docs.
next_steps: Redwood to send surge modeling spreadsheet and preliminary pricing (Maya) by 2025-05-20
Customer to provide 7-day token distribution and 95th percentile latency target (Ravi) by 2025-05-19
Schedule deeper SE-led benchmark call to validate KV cache behavior (Jordan + Ana) week of 5/26
action_items: Maya Patel: Share dedicated pricing + surge model spreadsheet — due 2025-05-20
Jordan Li: Arrange benchmark runbook and sample harness for KV/prefix caching — due 2025-05-23
Ravi Menon: Export 7-day token volume histogram and list of peak windows — due 2025-05-19
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-16 15:00 PDT
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood Solutions Eng), Ravi (StableCore Head of Platform), Ana (SRE Lead), Liam (CTO), Sofia (Infra PM)

Summary: quick intro, context on StableCore's production LLM routing, questions about reserved nodes, isolation, burst pre-warm and onprem options.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'll kick it off — i'm maya from redwood, this is jordan and priya on the eng side. how are folks doing?
[00:15] Ravi: good thanks, busy week but excited to get into this. we run inference for our moderation and personalization models, mostly transformer decoders, mixed seq lengths, a lot of amortized short responses but occasional long-form generation.
[00:35] Ana: yeah we see steady baseline but spikes around marketing campaigns, typically a few 10s of minutes, sometimes a couple hours.
[00:50] Jordan: thanks. can you share ballpark RPS and token counts? that really helps sizing reserved pools and pre-warm warm pools.
[01:05] Liam: ballpark — baseline 120 rps, avg tokens per call 25, peak windows we hit 2k rps for 8-12 minutes during launches. not every model is latency critical, S L O of 200-300 ms tail for some flows though.
[01:30] Priya: got it. when you say 2k rps is that all single tenant or multi-tenant mix?
[01:42] Ravi: it's mostly single tenant but we run multiple services per team. we want isolation so noisy neighbors don't push up tails. that's why we're evaluating reserved GPUs.
[02:00] Maya: makes sense. two questions we usually ask: do you need physical tenancy (dedicated hardware) or logical isolation (tenant fencing/hotpool)? and what's your spike profile — frequency and duration?
[02:15] Sofia: important note — compliance wants audit logs and K M S integration if we go private. also exploring onprem for regulated data, but hosting could be fine if we can meet encryption at rest + key control.
[02:34] Jordan: okay, from an ops perspective we can offer dedicated capacity with tenant fencing and warm pools. we typically recommend a combination: reserved nodes sized for baseline steady throughput + a hot-pool of prewarmed nodes for short spikes. hot-pool is prewarmed to hold KV cache for common prompts, reduces cold-start token penalty.
[02:58] Ana: how big is the prewarm cost usually? does it multiply our capacity cost by a lot?
[03:10] Jordan: depends on the hotpool sizing. small hotpool that covers your 95th percentile spike can be modest. for 2k rps 10 minute windows you'd likely need X nodes, we'll model it. caching helps a lot, prefix reuse reduces per-token work.
[03:30] Ravi: can you explain KV cache behavior — we saw in a previous vendor that recurring conversation contexts didn't stick, K V cash kept flushing.
[03:45] Priya: lol yeah i've seen K V cash mis-transcribes — in our runtime the KV cache is preserved when the session routes to the same worker; with warm-pools we also use sticky routing for short sessions to keep the cache hot. for multi-tenant we can pin a session to a reserved worker for a TTL.
[04:05] Liam: what about eviction? if a hotpool is saturated will you fallback to hosted model and incur higher latency?
[04:18] Jordan: we define fallback policies — either queue, spill to compatible lower-cost variant, or burst to shared capacity. we can set per-route SLO rules. for critical flows we recommend reserved + fallback to a smaller-quantized model with similar behavior.
[04:36] Ana: quantization worries us — we need output parity checks for critical moderation flows.
[04:45] Maya: understood — we can run A/B evals and regressions as part of rollout; redwood optimize flags regressions on prompt sets.
[04:58] Ravi: security: SSO integration (SAML), role-based access and audit trails are must-haves. and for private/onprem path we need H S M K M S integration.
[05:12] Maya: we support SAML SSO + RBAC and have audit logs. for private deployments we integrate with K M S or H S M, and produce the compliance pack. i'll send the SOC2 + architecture diagram after.
[05:27] Sofia: good. one more: burst accounting — how do you bill for hot-pool usage during spikes? is it amortized or per-minute?
[05:39] Maya: dedicated is typically a reservation for a pool (monthly commit) plus a small overage model. hot-pool prewarm can be part of the reservation or configured as burst credits — we'll share pricing tiers in the spreadsheet.
[05:55] Jordan: technical deep dive — on sizing: if your baseline is 120 rps and peaks 2k for 10 mins, we simulate multiple spike patterns: single big bursts, repeated short bursts and diurnal patterns. we look at median seq-len, token distributions and concurrency to map to device capacity and expected latency.
[06:20] Ana: can you do deterministic bench with our workload? we want to validate tail latencies with our prompts and truncation lengths.
[06:31] Jordan: yes, we'll run a pilot with your prompt set on a dedicated node or compatible local harness. small note — if you need onprem we can provide an onprem package but it does change the lead time and support model.
[06:48] Ravi: lead time — how long to provision dedicated pools and hotpool?
[06:53] Maya: for hosted dedicated it's usually 2-4 weeks once contract signed for standard sizes; for onprem it can be 6-10 weeks depending on procurement and H W shipping.
[07:06] Liam: one worry is eviction / preemption during cloud maintenance windows — we need SLA guarantees.
[07:14] Maya: Dedicated includes SLA-backed uptime and predictable throughput, we can include blackout windows in the contract. for critical flows we also recommend cross-region fallback to reduce maintenance impact.
[07:30] Ravi: are there any architecture constraints for our K8s platform? we run a custom inference gateway and currently use a shared replica pool of on-call instances.
[07:42] Jordan: Redwood exposes a standard REST/SDK; for private we can integrate with your control plane via a sidecar or a lightweight agent. we also support direct traffic routing to dedicate nodes using our routing policy hooks.
[07:58] Priya: question about multi-model mixing — we have some large models (40B) for summarization and smaller models for classification. can they share reserved pools?
[08:10] Jordan: mixing is possible but we recommend model variants per pool to avoid OOM and kernel mismatch. if they must share, we use soft isolation and QoS to prevent oversized models from evicting others. dedicated per-model-family is safest.
[08:28] Ana: telemetry / observability — we need token-level cost breakdowns and trace hooks.
[08:35] Maya: that's in the console — per-route/model dashboards, token breakouts, and tracing hooks you can ship to your APM.
[08:45] Ravi: okay let's talk numbers — can you walk us through a sample sizing calc now?
[08:52] Jordan: rough calc: baseline 120 rps * 25 tokens * 60 sec = tokens per minute etc — but quick version, mapping to node capacity depends on model type and batchability. for your 40B summarizer the node throughput is lower so separate pool. i'd propose: reserved baseline nodes sized to handle 200 rps with headroom, hot-pool sized to absorb 2k short bursts with sticky routing and TTL 12 minutes.
[09:20] Liam: does warm pool maintain KV across requests if session routes bounce? you mentioned sticky routing earlier but what's TTL and collision behavior?
[09:30] Jordan: TTL is configurable. typical TTL 10-15 minutes. collisions we evict based on LRU and weight by session importance. for dedicated pools you can pin sessions to the same worker for the TTL window to keep KV.
[09:45] Ana: in previous vendor we had long tail due to unlucky scheduling — how do you control batch sizes to meet tail S L O?
[09:55] Jordan: continuous batching with latency SLO shaping. you can set target latency and the runtime will limit batch sizes or spill to more workers to keep the tail in range.
[10:08] Ravi: any pitfalls customers see when moving from hosted to dedicated?
[10:14] Maya: two big ones — underestimating peak frequency (so hot-pool too small) and not accounting for model mix OOMs. we help with a pilot and profiling to avoid both.
[10:26] Sofia: curious about cost tradeoffs: if we overcommit reserved nodes is it easy to scale down?
[10:34] Maya: contracts usually have commit windows; we do offer burst credits and autoscaling patterns but committed capacity is for predictability. we can model step-down schedules for renewals.
[10:44] Ana: what about backups for private deployments — if onprem node fails how do we fail over to hosted?
[10:51] Jordan: we support hybrid fallback: if onprem fail, control plane can route to Redwood hosted or Dedicated in a different region. data residency and encryption keys handling are flagged — you'll want K M S replication or transient encryption for the fallback path.
[11:10] Liam: ok this is helpful. next concrete ask: we'll share 7-day traffic histograms and representative prompt sets. you'll send pricing and surge model. after that we want a hands-on benchmark.
[11:24] Maya: perfect — i'll send the SOC2/compliance docs + pricing spreadsheet + surge modeling by tuesday. jordan will own the benchmark runbook.
[11:34] Ravi: one logistical — we have procurement wanting a simple one-pager on support SLAs and escalation paths. can you attach that?
[11:41] Maya: yes i'll include a support SLA one-pager.
[11:46] Priya: i'll include a note on KV cache behavior and example sticky routing config in the runbook.
[11:55] Ana: anything else from redwood?
[11:58] Jordan: nothing else from me, we'll prepare the bench and align on prompts.
[12:05] Maya: great, thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule.

End of transcript. Note: occasional transcription errors e.g., K V cash, sam el etc. Natural speech, interruptions and clarifying questions present.
